name: Dochula Pass
tagline: 108 chortens and a Himalayan skyline on the Punakha road
meta_description: Dochula Pass guide: the 108 Druk Wangyal chortens, Druk Wangyal Lhakhang, Himalayan views Oct–Feb, Lungchutse hike, botanical park, 13 December tshechu.
summary: Dochula is the 3,100 m pass on the road from Thimphu to Punakha, about 22 km and 45 minutes from the capital. It holds the 108 Druk Wangyal chortens, a temple completed in 2008 and, from October to February, a view of the eastern Himalaya including Gangkar Puensum. Most visitors stop for 45 minutes; hikers stay half a day.
intro: The road east from Thimphu climbs through blue pine and hemlock for about 45 minutes before it tops out at Dochula, 3,100 m above sea level. On the crest, on a rounded hill, stand 108 white chortens with red bands, arranged in three rings around the slope, and above them a temple, Druk Wangyal Lhakhang. Prayer flags snap in the wind. On clear days between October and February the northern skyline opens up into a long line of snow peaks, including Gangkar Puensum, Bhutan's highest mountain at 7,570 m.

Almost every visitor to Punakha stops here, so the pass can be busy around midday. Come early or late and it is quiet. There is a café with big windows, toilets, and a viewpoint marked with the names of the peaks. A short walk around the chortens takes 20 minutes; the temple, with its modern murals of Bhutanese history, another 20. For more time, the Royal Botanical Park at Lamperi just below the pass has rhododendron gardens and forest trails, and a hiking path climbs from the pass to Lungchutse temple for a wider view.

Dochula's weather changes fast. In winter it can snow and the road may ice over, though it is usually cleared within hours. In the monsoon from June to September cloud often hides everything. October to February is the season for views, March to May for rhododendrons in the forest. Bring a warm layer at any time of year: it is often 8–10 °C colder here than in Punakha below. Dochula needs no separate permit; it lies on the Thimphu–Punakha route covered by your route permit.

story.title: Why 108 chortens stand on the pass
paras: In December 2003 the Royal Bhutan Army, led by the Fourth King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, launched an operation to remove camps that Indian insurgent groups had set up in the forests of southern Bhutan. The groups, from Assam and north Bengal, had used Bhutanese territory for years. The operation was brief and the camps were cleared. Bhutanese soldiers were killed, and the country chose to remember them, and all lives lost on both sides, with a monument of peace rather than triumph.

The 108 chortens, known as the Druk Wangyal Chortens, were built by Queen Ashi Dorji Wangmo Wangchuck and consecrated in June 2004. They rise in three tiers, 45 at the base, 36 in the middle and 27 at the top; 108 is a sacred number in Buddhism. The Druk Wangyal Lhakhang above them was completed in June 2008 to mark a century of the Wangchuck monarchy, and each year on 13 December the Druk Wangyal Tshechu is danced on the pass to commemorate the 2003 events.
story.source: Wikipedia, 'Dochula Pass' (chortens consecrated 19–20 June 2004; lhakhang completed 2008; tshechu on 13 December)

did_you_know: The 108 chortens at Dochula are arranged in three tiers of 45, 36 and 27.
Gangkar Puensum, visible from Dochula on clear days, is about 7,570 m high and is often cited as the highest unclimbed mountain in the world.
The Druk Wangyal Tshechu is held on Dochula every 13 December, a fixed date rather than a lunar one.
facts: 108 chortens, Himalayan panorama, Druk Wangyal Tshechu

highlights.title: The 108 Druk Wangyal Chortens
highlights.text: Built by Queen Ashi Dorji Wangmo Wangchuck and consecrated in 2004 in memory of soldiers who died in the December 2003 operation in southern Bhutan. Walk clockwise around the three tiers; the circuit takes 15–20 minutes and is free.

highlights.title: The Himalayan skyline
highlights.text: From October to February, mornings often bring a clear view north to a long chain of peaks including Gangkar Puensum, 7,570 m. A board at the viewpoint names the summits. Arrive before 9 am; cloud usually builds by late morning.

highlights.title: Druk Wangyal Lhakhang
highlights.text: The temple above the chortens was completed in 2008 to mark 100 years of the monarchy. Its murals mix traditional deities with scenes from modern Bhutanese history, including the Fourth King, which is unusual and worth a slow look.

highlights.title: Lungchutse temple hike
highlights.text: A forest trail climbs from near the pass to Lungchutse temple at about 3,500 m in 1.5–2 hours, through rhododendron and moss-hung trees, with a wider mountain view at the top. A good half-day for fit walkers; take your guide.

highlights.title: Royal Botanical Park, Lamperi
highlights.text: A short drive down the Punakha side, this protected forest of about 47 sq km has rhododendron gardens, walking trails and a small lake. Spring, March to May, is best when dozens of rhododendron species flower. Entry about Nu 100, indicative 2026.

highlights.title: Tea and a view at the Dochula café
highlights.text: The café beside the chortens has wide windows facing north, so on a clear day you can sit with tea and look at the mountains. Prices are higher than in town but fair for the setting, about ₹100–250 for tea and a snack.

how_to_reach.text: Dochula is about 22 km and 45 minutes from Thimphu on the road to Punakha. It is almost always visited as a stop on that drive. A car with driver costs ₹4,500–6,500 a day, indicative 2026, with a licensed guide. The Thimphu–Punakha route permit covers it; check current status before you travel.

If you are not continuing to Punakha, a half-day trip from Thimphu works: leave at 7 am for the morning view, walk the chortens, and return by lunch. In winter, ask the guide to check for snow on the road before setting out.
Buses between Thimphu and Punakha pass over Dochula but do not stop long. As a tourist you would need your guide with you, so a hired car is the practical choice.

where_to_stay: Most visitors do not stay at Dochula; it is a stop between Thimphu (45 minutes away) and Punakha (1.5–2 hours below). Stay in Thimphu if you want to reach the pass at dawn for the clearest mountain view, or in Punakha if you are heading east. The Dochula area has very limited accommodation, so we do not recommend planning a night on the pass itself. Hotel Druk in Thimphu and Dhensa Boutique Resort in Punakha are on either side.
costs: Tea and snack at the café
budget_tip: Leave Thimphu at 7 am rather than 10 am: the mountain view is clearer, the café is empty, and you still reach Punakha for lunch without paying for an extra half-day of car hire.
tips: Carry a warm jacket even in spring; the pass is usually 8–10 °C colder than Punakha.
Stop on the way to Punakha, not the way back, because mornings give the best chance of clear views.
Walk the chortens clockwise and do not climb on them for photographs.
In winter the road can have snow or ice; your driver may fit chains or wait for clearing. Check current status before you travel.
If you visit on 13 December, arrive early for the Druk Wangyal Tshechu; parking fills fast.

experiences.title: The 108 chortens and the morning mountain view
experiences.summary: A memorial of 108 chortens on a 3,100 m pass, with a temple above and a line of Himalayan peaks to the north. Most travellers give it 15 minutes; we explain why 45 is better and how to time it for a clear sky.
body: Park at the pass and walk up among the chortens. There are 108 of them, white with a red band, set on a mound in three tiers of 45, 36 and 27. Queen Ashi Dorji Wangmo Wangchuck had them built after the December 2003 operation in which the Royal Bhutan Army cleared Indian insurgent camps from southern Bhutan; they were consecrated in June 2004. They honour the soldiers who died and are meant as a monument of peace.

Walk around them clockwise. Each tier gives a different angle, and the prayer flags strung between trees make the scene. Then turn north. From October to February the sky is often clear in the early morning and you see a long chain of peaks across the horizon. The highest is Gangkar Puensum, about 7,570 m, Bhutan's highest mountain and one of the highest in the world never to have been climbed, since Bhutan banned mountaineering on high peaks.

Time it right. Leave Thimphu by 7 am and you reach the pass before the cloud builds. Midday usually brings haze and tour buses. A board at the viewpoint names the peaks. The chortens are free. On 13 December the Druk Wangyal Tshechu fills the pass with masked dancers. Take care on the steps in winter, when they can be icy, and keep a warm jacket on, as the wind is cold even when the sun is out.

faqs.q: Why are there 108 chortens at Dochula
faqs.a: They were built by Queen Ashi Dorji Wangmo Wangchuck to honour Bhutanese soldiers who died in the December 2003 operation against Indian insurgent camps in southern Bhutan. The number 108 is sacred in Buddhism. They were consecrated in June 2004 and stand in three tiers of 45, 36 and 27.

faqs.q: Can I see the Himalayas from Dochula
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days, mostly from October to February in the early morning. The view stretches across a range of peaks including Gangkar Puensum, about 7,570 m. In spring there is often haze, and from June to September cloud usually hides the mountains. Arrive before 9 am for the best chance.

faqs.q: How much time should I spend at Dochula
faqs.a: About 45 minutes to an hour: 20 minutes walking the chortens, 15 minutes at the viewpoint and 15–20 minutes in the temple, plus tea at the café. Add half a day for the Lungchutse hike or an hour for the Royal Botanical Park at Lamperi.

experiences.title: Druk Wangyal Lhakhang and its modern murals
experiences.summary: The temple above the 108 chortens was completed in 2008 to mark a century of Bhutan's monarchy. Its murals put kings, soldiers and modern history alongside the usual deities, which makes it one of the more unusual temples in the country.
body: Druk Wangyal Lhakhang stands on the slope just above the chortens. It was completed in June 2008, the year Bhutan marked 100 years of the Wangchuck monarchy and adopted its constitution. The building is traditional in form, with a gilded roof and painted woodwork, and sits with the forest behind it and the mountain view in front.

Inside, the paintings mix the classical with the contemporary. Alongside the Buddhas and protective deities you will find scenes from Bhutan's recent history, including the Fourth King, and images that recall the 2003 operation in the south. Most Bhutanese temples show only religious subjects, so this mix is worth taking time over. Ask your guide to explain the figures, because they tie the 108 chortens outside to the country's modern story.

Remove shoes and caps inside, dress modestly and do not take photographs of the interior. The temple is generally open in daytime; an attendant may be present. On 13 December each year the Druk Wangyal Tshechu is held in the open ground in front, with masked dances that commemorate the 2003 events. It is one of the few tshechus on a fixed calendar date, so it is easy to plan around.

faqs.q: When was Druk Wangyal Lhakhang built
faqs.a: It was completed in June 2008, the year Bhutan celebrated 100 years of the Wangchuck monarchy and adopted its first written constitution. It stands above the 108 Druk Wangyal chortens at Dochula, which had been consecrated in 2004.

faqs.q: What is the Druk Wangyal Tshechu
faqs.a: A festival of masked dances held at Dochula every 13 December, commemorating the December 2003 operation that cleared insurgent camps from southern Bhutan. Unlike most tshechus it follows the Western calendar, so the date does not move. It is free to watch; arrive early for parking and a place to stand.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Druk Wangyal Lhakhang
faqs.a: No. As in other Bhutanese temples, photography inside is not allowed. You can photograph the exterior, the chortens and the mountain view freely. Remove shoes and caps before entering and keep your voice low if prayers are under way.

experiences.title: Hike from Dochula to Lungchutse temple
experiences.summary: A forest climb from near Dochula to a small temple on a ridge at about 3,500 m, with a wider view of the Himalaya than from the pass itself. A good half-day for fit walkers on the Thimphu–Punakha drive.
body: The trail starts near the Dochula pass and climbs through a forest of rhododendron, hemlock and fir hung with grey-green lichen. The path is clear but steady, gaining roughly 400 m in 1.5–2 hours. Prayer flags mark the higher sections. In spring, from March to May, the rhododendrons flower red, pink and white along the way; in autumn the forest is quiet and the views open up as you climb.

Lungchutse temple sits on the ridge top at about 3,500 m. It is small and simply kept, and on a clear day the view north takes in a broad sweep of the eastern Himalaya, often better than the view from the pass because you are above the trees. Some walkers continue on longer trails along the ridge; your guide will know the options and the state of the path.

Start early to beat the cloud, carry water, snacks and a warm layer, and wear walking shoes with grip, as the path can be muddy or frosty. Allow 3–4 hours round trip. A licensed guide must accompany you. The hike is free. It suits teenagers and fit adults; people coming straight from the plains should acclimatise in Thimphu or Paro for a day or two first, because 3,500 m is high enough to feel.

faqs.q: How hard is the Lungchutse hike from Dochula
faqs.a: Moderate. It is a steady climb of about 400 m from near the pass to the temple at roughly 3,500 m, taking 1.5–2 hours up and about an hour down. The path is clear but can be muddy or icy. Acclimatise in Thimphu or Paro first and go at an easy pace.

faqs.q: Is the view from Lungchutse better than Dochula
faqs.a: Often, yes. The temple stands higher on the ridge and above much of the forest, so the view north to the Himalaya is wider. As at the pass, mornings from October to February give the best chance of a clear sky. Cloud usually builds by midday.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Lungchutse hike
faqs.a: Yes. Under the April 2026 Department of Tourism notification, all tourists travel with a licensed guide beyond the first checkpoint. Your trip guide can walk with you. The trail itself is free. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Rhododendrons at the Royal Botanical Park
experiences.best_time: Mar–May for flowers; Oct–Nov for birds
experiences.summary: Just below Dochula on the Punakha side, the Royal Botanical Park at Lamperi protects about 47 sq km of forest with rhododendron gardens, a small lake and walking trails. In spring it is one of the best places in Bhutan to see rhododendrons in flower.
body: The Royal Botanical Park lies at Lamperi, a few kilometres below Dochula on the road towards Punakha. It covers about 47 sq km of temperate forest of oak, hemlock, fir and rhododendron, and was set up as Bhutan's first botanical park. A visitor centre near the gate explains the forest and its plants. Trails of different lengths lead into the woods, from a 30-minute loop to longer walks of several hours.

Spring is the season to come. From March to May dozens of rhododendron species flower across the park, in colours from deep red to pale yellow and white, with magnolia and primula among them. The park holds a rhododendron festival in spring in some years; check if it is on during your dates. Birders come in autumn and spring for laughingthrushes, pheasants and other forest species. Monkeys and red pandas live in the wider area, though sightings are rare.

Entry is about Nu 100, indicative 2026. Wear walking shoes and a warm layer, as it is cold and damp in the shade. The park is a good stop when cloud hides the mountains at the pass, because forest walks do not depend on views. Combine it with Dochula on the way to Punakha; allow 1.5 hours for a short walk and the visitor centre, longer for a proper hike.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom at Dochula
faqs.a: Mainly from March to May. Different species flower at different times, so early spring brings some red varieties and late spring others. The Royal Botanical Park at Lamperi below the pass is the best place to see many species together. In some years a rhododendron festival is held there in spring.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for the Royal Botanical Park in Bhutan
faqs.a: About Nu 100 per person, indicative 2026, payable at the gate near Lamperi below Dochula. Rupees are accepted at par. Walking the trails is included. Check current status before you travel, as fees are revised from time to time.

faqs.q: Can I see red pandas at the Royal Botanical Park
faqs.a: Red pandas live in this kind of temperate forest, but they are shy and sightings are rare. Do not plan a visit around them. You are more likely to see birds such as laughingthrushes and pheasants, especially in early morning. A local bird guide improves your chances.

faqs.q: How high is Dochula Pass
faqs.a: About 3,100 m above sea level, on the road between Thimphu and Punakha. It is the highest point of that drive. People coming straight from the plains may feel the altitude a little; walk slowly around the chortens and drink water. Most visitors spend 45 minutes to an hour here.

faqs.q: How far is Dochula from Thimphu
faqs.a: About 22 km, a 45-minute drive east of Thimphu on the road to Punakha. From Dochula it is another 1.5–2 hours down to Punakha. Most travellers stop at the pass on the way to Punakha rather than making a separate trip.

faqs.q: Does Dochula get snow
faqs.a: Yes, often between December and February, and occasionally in March. The road can ice over and may close briefly until it is cleared. Snow also makes the chortens and the view beautiful. Your driver will know the conditions; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Dochula
faqs.a: No. The pass, the 108 chortens and the views are free. The Royal Botanical Park at Lamperi below the pass charges about Nu 100, indicative 2026. The café charges for tea and snacks. You do need your licensed guide and the Punakha route permit to be on this road.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Dochula
faqs.a: Early morning from October to February, when the sky is clearest and the Himalaya is visible. March to May is best for rhododendrons in the forest, though views are often hazy. In the monsoon, June to September, cloud usually covers the pass.

faqs.q: Which mountains can you see from Dochula
faqs.a: On clear days, a long chain of peaks across northern Bhutan, including Gangkar Puensum, at about 7,570 m Bhutan's highest mountain. A signboard at the viewpoint names the main summits. The clearest days are in winter mornings; cloud often builds by late morning.

faqs.q: Are there toilets and food at Dochula
faqs.a: Yes. There is a café beside the chortens with tea, coffee, snacks and simple meals, and toilets nearby. Prices are a little higher than in Thimphu, around ₹100–250 for tea and a snack, indicative 2026. It is the only real stop on the Thimphu–Punakha road.

faqs.q: Is Dochula worth visiting in the monsoon
faqs.a: Only as a short stop on the way to Punakha. From June to September cloud and mist usually hide the mountains and often the chortens themselves. The atmosphere can be lovely in drifting mist, but do not make a separate trip for it. Check road conditions for landslides.

faqs.q: Why is Gangkar Puensum unclimbed
faqs.a: Bhutan banned mountaineering on peaks above 6,000 m in 1994, out of respect for local beliefs that the mountains are the homes of deities, and later banned it altogether. Earlier attempts in the 1980s failed. So Gangkar Puensum, about 7,570 m, is widely cited as the highest unclimbed mountain in the world.
